**For repeatable comparison images, I’d shortlist LVGL’s converter, FreeType, and monobit.** The best choice depends on whether you’re starting with outline fonts such as TTF/OTF, or existing bitmap fonts such as BDF/FNT/PSF.

| Option | Useful for | Image output and limitations |
|---|---|---|
| **[LVGL Font Converter](https://lvgl.io/tools/fontconverter)** / **[lv_font_conv](https://github.com/lvgl/lv_font_conv)** | Converting outline fonts for embedded displays | Supports **1 bpp**. The CLI’s `--format dump` exports individual glyph images plus JSON metrics. You would compose those into text specimens or comparison sheets. |
| **[FreeType](https://freetype.org/freetype2/docs/reference/ft2-glyph_retrieval.html)** | Controlled comparisons of rasterization and hinting | Explicit monochrome rendering through `FT_RENDER_MODE_MONO`, with control over hinting and embedded bitmap selection. Requires a small rendering harness to create PNG comparison sheets. |
| **[Python + Pillow](https://pillow.readthedocs.io/en/stable/reference/ImageDraw.html#PIL.ImageDraw.ImageDraw.fontmode)** | Quickly generating labeled, side-by-side text samples | `draw.fontmode = "1"` disables antialiasing. Convenient for PNG composition; direct FreeType offers more control over rasterization settings. |
| **[monobit](https://github.com/robhagemans/monobit)** | Comparing fonts that **already contain bitmap glyphs** | Reads many bitmap formats, including BDF, FON/FNT and PSF. Exports PNG glyph sheets and annotated charts. My first choice for existing bitmap fonts. |
| **[FontForge](https://fontforge.org/docs/tutorial/editexample8.html)** | Generating and inspecting bitmap strikes from outline fonts | Creates strikes at selected pixel sizes and supports bitmap editing. Its scripting interface can export glyph images from existing strikes; composing comparison sheets takes another step. |
| **[SnowB BMF](https://snowb.org/en/docs/)** — online | Quickly producing bitmap atlases in a browser | Imports outline fonts, offers preview and sharpness controls, and exports PNG atlases with metrics. Useful for exploration; verify the exported pixels are binary for a strict 1-bit comparison. |
| **[truetype2gfx](https://rop.nl/truetype2gfx/)** — online | Trying outline fonts for Adafruit GFX | Lets you choose/upload fonts, set size and enter demo text. Convenient for quick inspection; primarily a GFX font converter rather than a comparison-image exporter. |
| **[AngelCode BMFont](https://angelcode.com/products/bmfont/)** — Windows | Generating glyph atlases with Windows rendering | Exports PNG textures and metrics, supports disabling font smoothing and command-line generation. Its output is an atlas rather than a readable text comparison sheet. |

For interactive investigation, FreeType also provides **[`ftview` and `ftdiff`](https://freetype.org/freetype2/docs/tutorial/step2.html)**: useful for exploring rendering and hinting differences before deciding what to capture.

**For your Glypherie work, there’s also the existing repository pipeline.** It already publishes native-resolution monochrome specimen PNGs and aligned previous/current/difference glyph images. The documented commands are `just specimens` and `just comparisons`; see the [generator README](/Users/dimitri/Documents/Code/personal/Inkplate/font_generator/tools/generator/README.md:141). That is probably the easiest place to compose external reference renders alongside your own.

One important distinction: **native monochrome rasterization and thresholding a grayscale render are different comparison conditions.** FreeType exposes monochrome-specific rendering and hinting settings, so record those settings alongside font size. For useful comparisons, keep text, baseline and placement consistent, and show both native-size images and integer nearest-neighbor enlargements. [FreeType rendering documentation](https://freetype.org/freetype2/docs/reference/ft2-glyph_retrieval.html)

For **existing TTF → monochrome sample text**, I’d recommend these:

| Option | When I’d choose it | Main limitation |
|---|---|---|
| **[Pillow](https://pillow.readthedocs.io/en/stable/reference/ImageDraw.html#PIL.ImageDraw.ImageDraw.fontmode)** | **Best default for generating comparison PNGs.** A short Python script can render paragraphs, multiple fonts and sizes, labels and enlarged views. Set `draw.fontmode = "1"` for monochrome text. | Limited control over FreeType’s hinting settings. |
| **[FreeType directly](https://freetype.org/freetype2/docs/reference/ft2-glyph_retrieval.html)** | **Best for evaluating rasterization quality.** Explicitly compare native font hints, autohinting and unhinted rendering with `FT_RENDER_MODE_MONO`. | Requires code to lay out text and compose images. |
| **[truetype2gfx](https://rop.nl/truetype2gfx/)** | **Best quick online option.** Upload your TTF, enter sample text and inspect it on a simulated display. | Primarily exports Adafruit font data. Sizes use points with a 141-DPI convention, so don’t equate its size setting with pixels. |
| **[LVGL converter + LVGL simulator](https://github.com/lvgl/lv_font_conv)** | **Best when you want to reproduce actual LVGL text.** Convert at 1 bpp, render a label in LVGL and capture the result. | More setup; the converter alone exports glyphs rather than a composed text image. |

**My choice for your comparison work: Pillow for convenient specimen generation; direct FreeType when hinting and rasterization settings are part of what you’re comparing.** Use the LVGL route when matching the eventual device rendering matters.

content.text:
**For that, I recommend ImageMagick:** one command renders your TTF and sample text directly into a monochrome PNG.

```sh
magick -background white -fill black \
  -font ./font.ttf -density 72 -pointsize 16 +antialias \
  -size 600x caption:'Your sentence or paragraph goes here.' \
  sample.png
```

This produces a 600-pixel-wide image with automatic wrapping and height. At 72 DPI, `-pointsize 16` corresponds to 16 pixels per em. For a single unwrapped line, remove `-size 600x` and replace `caption:` with `label:`. [Text rendering documentation](https://usage.imagemagick.org/text/)

**For an online preview**, use [truetype2gfx](https://rop.nl/truetype2gfx/): upload the TTF and enter your sentence. ImageMagick is more convenient when you need saved comparison images.
